title: Public and Private Subnets knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which item is directly listed as a subtopic of “Public and Private Subnets”?
options: A deployment choice that has no relationship to the named AWS topic
A reason to skip identity, testing or cleanup controls
A concept outside this lesson's stated scope
questions.explanation: The PDF explicitly lists “Public subnet routing requirements” under lesson 46, “Public and Private Subnets”. The other choices are unrelated distractors.

questions.prompt: Which approach best fits “Public and Private Subnets” in a safe AWS workflow?
options: Assume a successful screen or one run proves availability and security.
Check route tables and all required network controls from source to destination.
Use one broad permanent credential and avoid documenting assumptions.
Deploy first and check permissions, logs and costs only if something fails.
questions.answer_key: Check route tables and all required network controls from source to destination.
questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful; network ACLs are stateless and rule ordered.

questions.prompt: A workflow related to “Public and Private Subnets” behaves unexpectedly. What is the most useful next step?
options: Verify prerequisites and the resolved identity/Region, inspect the relevant resource state and logs, then change one variable at a time and retest.
Open all network paths and grant administrator permissions so the error disappears.
Repeat the same action indefinitely without inspecting logs or returned errors.
Assume the service is broken without checking quota, Region, routing or policy context.
questions.answer_key: Verify prerequisites and the resolved identity/Region, inspect the relevant resource state and logs, then change one variable at a time and retest.
questions.explanation: Troubleshooting should narrow the cause using prerequisites, identity/Region, resource state, logs and a controlled retest. Broad permissions and blind retries can introduce additional risk.
